speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I think you are very efficient, so the earlier Ministerial Statement has progressed very quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This has allowed us to become a vibrant business hub and an attractive investment destination.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We must remain open and continue to attract new investments so as to grow our economy and create good opportunities for our businesses and our people.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, we also recognise that the world has become increasingly complex and the economic environment more uncertain and challenging, creating new risks and vulnerabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We must constantly review and update our regulatory regime to keep pace with the changes in the global economic landscape and to strengthen the resilience of our economy in the face of new threats.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Doing so will give our investors and businesses added confidence in our economy and our ability to respond to emerging challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Indeed, as an open economy, we can be vulnerable to actors that may seek to undermine our national security interests through ownership and control of critical business entities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Therefore, we must put in place adequate measures to safeguard our national security interests.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In fact, we have been doing so through our sectoral legislation to mitigate such risks specific to the respective sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For instance, the Banking Act and Telecommunications Act require approval to be sought before a party acquires 12% of shares or voting power and before appointment of key personnel, such as the chief executive officer.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will help prevent actors from influencing critical entities in the financial and telecommunications sectors to undermine their stability and threaten our national security.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have taken a calibrated and balanced approach, which has enabled us to ride the winds of globalisation and benefit from the growth of the global economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In recent years, we have seen several global financial crises that threatened to undermine the stability of economies and societies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have lived through the COVID-19 pandemic that led to border restrictions and shortages of essential medical supplies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: There is also increased use of protectionist measures amidst geopolitical contestations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Military conflicts have also brought about disruptions to critical supplies, such as energy and food.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This has led to many countries prioritising domestic and national security considerations, leaning towards "near-shoring", "friend-shoring" and "re-shoring" of supply chains.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Against this backdrop, it is timely that we update our investment management toolkit to ensure it remains adequate and effective.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Investors in a critical entity will normally have some form of influence or control of the entity’s decisions and operations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Investors may then exploit their ownership and control over these entities to disrupt the delivery of essential goods and services, or access and use sensitive information to threaten our national security.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It is, therefore, important to have adequate and effective investment management measures to safeguard our national security and ensure our economy remains resilient.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will provide businesses and investors with continued confidence in Singapore as a stable, trusted and well-connected global business and investment hub.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: While the sectoral legislation we have today has served us well, we need to continually assess our security needs and strengthen our safeguards, where necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In designing this regime, we have studied the investment management legislation of other jurisdictions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have also taken into account our current sectoral legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Allow me to share three key principles in the design of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: First, the legislation should strike a careful balance between protecting our national security interests and minimising the impact on businesses and investors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Second, the Bill should apply to both foreign and local parties, while focusing on national security considerations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Third, the processes should be as transparent as possible, while taking into account national security considerations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: First, provisions that apply only to designated entities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Second, provisions that apply to entities that have acted against Singapore’s national security interests, regardless of whether they have been designated.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The first broad set of provisions relate only to ownership and control over designated entities to ensure the reliability of critical functions that they provide as well as to safeguard Singapore's national security interests.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is quite unique to Singapore, as most overseas jurisdictions generally scope the designation broadly to cover all entities based on either activities they carry out or the sectors they operate in.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Common overseas examples of these activities or sectors include those relating to communications, defence-related supply chains and advanced technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This approach was deliberately chosen to reduce the regulatory burden of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Otherwise, every entity that falls within certain sectors or provide certain activities would all be included, regardless of whether the entity itself is critical to our national security interests.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This would not only be administratively tedious but also impact Singapore's position as a business and investment hub.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Instead, our targeted approach to designate only specific entities will achieve a better balance between national security and the impact on businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In deciding which entities should be considered for designation, various factors will be considered.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These include whether the entity provides a critical function in relation to Singapore's national security interests, such as a key provider of security-related functions, especially where there are few or no alternatives; and whether it is adequately covered by existing sectoral legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Conversely, should a designated entity subsequently cease to meet these criteria, its designation may be cancelled.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Over the last few months, we have reached out to all the entities that are being considered for designation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: That means, if you have not been approached, you are not currently being considered.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The engagements will help us to better understand their perspectives and concerns, clarify the obligations should they eventually be designated and explore ways to mitigate the regulatory impact on their businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In the interest of transparency and to provide certainty to the entities and potential investors, clause 17 provides that all designations or cancellations of designation will be notified in the Gazette.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Clauses 18 to 20 allow the Minister to exercise oversight over the ownership or control changes involving parties in positions to influence and direct the actions of the designated entities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These requirements will not apply retroactively, but only to new ownership or control changes after the entities have been designated.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Notification or approval obligations will be imposed on prospective controllers, existing controllers and designated entities, based on specific thresholds that take reference from existing sectoral legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Parties are, similarly, required to seek Minister's approval if they are becoming an indirect controller or acquiring parts of the business or undertaking as a going concern.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: On the other hand, sellers will have to seek Minister's approval before ceasing to be a 50% or 75% controller.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Clause 16 allows the Minister the flexibility to vary such thresholds for specific entities as the situation warrants and, if so, to prescribe them in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Under clause 19, the Minister may approve applications by parties if he is satisfied that all of the following conditions are met.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: One, that the prospective acquirors or controllers and their associates are fit and proper persons.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Two, that the designated entity will be able to continue providing its critical functions if the transaction proceeds after approval is granted.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Three, that approving the transaction is not against Singapore's national security interests.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The designated entity has a duty to report changes in ownership or control specified above to the Minister within seven days of it becoming aware of the event.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This provides an additional safeguard to detect any potential attempts by parties to circumvent the notification and approval requirements and ensure that the entities stay vigilant to potential threats.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, materially affected parties may apply to the Minister to validate the transaction and the Minister may do so by issuing a validation notice.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Minister may also proactively issue such a notice if he is satisfied that it is in the interest of Singapore's national security to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Clauses 22 to 24 allow the Minister to issue remedial directions under a variety of circumstances – for example, if conditions of approval have been breached or false or misleading information was provided in relation to an application for approval.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Such remedial directions may include directing the transfer or disposal of equity interest in the designated entity or any other direction that the Minister considers appropriate.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Where a remedial direction has yet to be carried out, clause 25 has provisions to achieve the practical outcome of such a direction.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As an example, if an initial remedial direction to divest equity interest has not been carried out, voting rights may not be exercised and no dividends may be paid in relation to the relevant equity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Bill also includes oversight over the appointment of key personnel of the designated entities, such as the chief executive officer, board directors and chairperson of the board.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Such individuals can influence the entity's policies, decisions and actions, including over the critical functions it provides.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Under clause 27, a designated entity must obtain prior approval from the Minister to appoint key personnel.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Minister may consider any relevant factor in arriving at a decision.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, if we receive information that a particular individual has a track record of engaging in conduct or activities that could undermine our national security interests, then this would be taken into consideration in deciding whether approval would be granted.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Clause 28 allows the Minister to require the removal of an appointed key personnel of a designated entity, if this was done without the necessary approval or if any condition of approval has been breached.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Minister can also require the removal of any key personnel, if deemed necessary in the interest of national security.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: There are also provisions to ensure the continued performance of the critical functions by the designated entities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Under clause 26, the designated entities cannot be dissolved, terminated, wound up voluntarily or be subject to judicial management without the Minister's consent.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In addition, parties cannot enforce security, judgment or Court order over designated entities, unless prior advance notice has been given to the Minister.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will allow the Minister to take the necessary actions to safeguard our national security interests.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: If there are Court proceedings involved, the Minister will be a party to such proceedings and the Court must consider any representations made by the Minister.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Clauses 30 and 31 allow the Minister to issue Special Administration Orders – otherwise known as “step-in rights” – to direct the takeover of control of the affairs, businesses and property of a designated entity by another party.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Other orders can also be issued, such as directing the designated entity to immediately take or cease any action or appointing a person to advise the designated entity in the proper conduct of its businesses or undertaking.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: When exercising such powers, we will always be mindful of shareholders' interests.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The second broad set of provisions relate to powers that can be exercised against any entity that has acted against Singapore's national security interests, regardless of whether they are designated or not.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Currently, there are already existing laws to deal with egregious acts against national security.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, under the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act, the Court may order the winding up of a company if it is being used against Singapore's national security.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, winding up an entity could affect the continued provisioning of its functions, and may not be the desired outcome.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In the investment management legislation of most overseas jurisdictions, there are similar concepts often referred to as "call-in" powers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The relevant authorities may "call-in" certain types of transactions for review, even though they may not have triggered filing and pre-approval requirements under the regime.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Such "call-in" powers are typically exercised on national interest- or national security-related grounds.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In some jurisdictions, they can be based on perceived risks without actual actions committed by the entity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The time limits of such "call-in" powers vary across jurisdictions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, this could range from five years in the UK to 10 years in Australia, and there is no time limit in the US.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Following the review of the transaction, a range of directions may be issued, such as directing the transacting party to transfer or dispose of his equity interest in the entity; or directing the entity to restrict disclosure of confidential information to any person.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Under clause 12, powers under the Bill can be exercised against any individual regardless of their citizenship or residency status; and any entity, regardless of the type or domicile location.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As mentioned earlier, this takes into account that threats may emanate from various sources or channelled through various entities and we will need sufficient flexibility to exercise our legislative levers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Further, under clauses 17 and 32, entities that may be classified as designated entities, or for which post-transaction powers may apply, would include those that are incorporated, formed, or established in Singapore; carry out activities in Singapore; or provide goods and services to persons in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Clauses 47 to 50 provide a range of enforcement powers that authorised officers, Police officers and Commercial Affairs officers may exercise.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: All of them have powers to require any individual or entity to provide information relating to the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Police officers and Commercial Affairs officers will also have powers to enter premises for investigation under the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Penalties will be differentiated depending on whether the party guilty of the offence is an individual or an entity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Fixed monetary penalties may be insufficient deterrence for certain offences that are meant to safeguard our national security interests.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is especially so as the Bill would cover transactions across a wide range of values, as well as entities in diverse sectors and of different sizes as well as varying financial abilities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For high-value transactions or large businesses with significant revenue, a fixed penalty quantum may neither be a sufficient deterrent nor result in a proportionate penalty in the event of non-compliance.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: On the other hand, for low-value transactions or small-sized businesses, going with the transaction value or annual turnover alone could translate to penalty amounts that run into similar issues.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For individuals, imprisonment is also a possible penalty.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: While the penalties themselves are significant, they need to be an effective deterrent as we are dealing here with actions that may impact national security.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Clauses 40 to 45 provide details of the Reviewing Tribunal, while clause 46 provides for limited judicial review only on grounds of failure to comply with any procedural requirement of the Act, or the regulations or rules made under the Act.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These processes are modelled after similar provisions in other legislation here that deal with Singapore's national security interests, such as the Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Office will serve as a dedicated one-stop touchpoint to engage affected stakeholders and provide them with guidance and clarifications.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It will also coordinate and oversee the implementation of the Act.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In closing, I would like to take this opportunity to thank various industry representatives, such as those from the law firms, financial institutions, accountancy firms and general business community, which we have consulted and which have provided valuable input in helping us refine the Bill and take into account potential impact on businesses and investors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As described, the Bill intends to provide Singapore with an updated toolkit to manage threats posed by significant investments into critical entities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Singapore has always strived to be a responsible partner on the global stage.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our actions are based on clear and consistent principles.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will work closely with the industry and affected stakeholders and implement this Bill in a calibrated and balanced manner.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This approach will allow Singapore to remain a trusted and reliable business hub, where investors can continue to invest and operate with confidence and create more opportunities for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They are managed on commercial basis with the aim to attain profitability and other economic interests.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, I see the need for the Government to be empowered with the necessary legislative and executive levers to not only safeguard our national security, but also ensure resilience of our economy and society.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many other jurisdictions already have such dedicated regulations to monitor and manage such strategic entities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: When I first heard of this Bill, my immediate response was that I thought we already have these ownerships and control safeguards to manage key sectors, such as in telecommunications, banking, utilities and media, through very extensive legislation and regulations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, upon more detailed reading of the Bill and how the framework of review is designed, I am fully supportive of this targeted approach to review these specifically earmarked critical entities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The new legislation targets and imposes on individual entities, rather than on the whole sector or sets of activity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As there are already existing sectoral legislations to regulate the broader critical and strategic sectors, this Bill will only impact a handful of entities that are of significant strategic and security implications.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As the Minister said, those who are covered under the Bill would have been informed.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Those who are not, I suppose they can feel more assured now.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Furthermore, the designated entities will be published in the Gazette.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The security threats that we face could come from various sources and in various forms, including through the ownership and control of the critical entities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, the provisions in this Bill would apply to entities that are both locally- or foreign-owned.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Therefore, beyond imposing obligations tied to specific transactions relating to significant investments, the Bill also contains other important provisions, such as requiring approvals for the appointment of key personnels to the designated entity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Notwithstanding my support, I have a few clarifications to seek from the Minister.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, my question to the Minister is, whether entities, especially those in new or emerging sectors, like artificial intelligence (AI); or those providing services in certain sectors, such as data centres, will be designated under the Bill?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As the Minister has said, the Bill was also developed in consultation with various industry representatives from the legal, finance and accounting sectors, as well the general business community, with particular attention paid to minimising the potential impact on businesses and investors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, overall, I find the Bill suitably balanced between maintaining an open investment environment while still fulfilling the intent to have adequate and effective safeguards for Singapore's national security needs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In recent years, the issue of national security has risen in prominence, alongside greater uncertainty and volatility in the world today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To that end, I agree with the importance of safeguarding critical entities and infrastructure in Singapore and in taking preventive and corrective actions to keep our country safe and secure from state versus non-state actors, conventional versus non-conventional threats alike.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Many countries similarly recognise this point and have moved towards enacting or strengthening similar laws in recent years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While we have learnt in Economics 101 that globalisation and free trade drives significant gains for both trading partners, I believe that there could be other important policy objectives that the Government must deliver for its people, such as minimising income and wealth inequality and ensuring that the gains of economic growth accrue broadly, ensuring our supply chains are resilient as evidenced by COVID-19, to name a few.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While global trade continues to grow, trade-offs to international trade are now seen by an increasing number of economies as almost inevitable, in favour of stability and national security.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Findings from a September 2023 World Trade Organization (WTO) report, for example, suggest that trade is gradually becoming re-oriented along geopolitical lines.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But we can also see for ourselves the trade tensions between the two largest economies of the world and how they have cascading effects on the investment environment globally, and how corporate merger and acquisition (M&A) transactions have been blocked in the interests of national security.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Economic Development Board (EDB) sums it up pretty well, in that "The Singapore Government is committed to creating a pro-business environment through its economic and manpower policies".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This has also been affirmed in the Economist Intelligence Unit's (EIU's) latest business environment rankings, with Singapore retaining its position as the world's best business environment for 15 consecutive years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet despite our pro-business environment and open economy with the ease of movement of goods, services, labour and capital, in speaking to international investors over the years, a number have shared with me their wonder as to how the Government continues to be able to exercise control over businesses and workers alike.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the case of workers, the rules imposed on trade union administration and leadership, or in Prime Minister’s words, a "symbiotic relationship between the People's Action Party (PAP) and the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC)".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And in the case of businesses, explicit control mechanisms and arguably influence over companies, even though they may not be state-owned enterprises per se.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, Singapore Airlines has one non-tradeable special share issued to the Ministry of Finance (MOF) and no resolution may be passed on certain undisclosed matters without prior written approval of the MOF.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For SingPost, the appointment of the Chairman, Directors and Group CEO requires the prior written approval of the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), in addition to other Postal Services Act obligations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Singapore Press Holdings, when it was listed then, had a small handful of shareholders holding management shares; and though these represent only 1% of total issued shares, had 68% of the total votes when it comes to any resolution relating to the appointment or dismissal of a director or any member of staff.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These are just some examples of listed companies with publicly available disclosures detailing such mechanisms, but there could well be more of such mechanisms for other public or private companies in Singapore that we may not know of.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Would these companies and the specifics of their control provisions be subsequently encompassed under SIRA and would the Minister be able to confirm if such details will be made public in the interest of transparency?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, it is unclear whether the list of designated entities will eventually be disclosed.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moving to my next point, as I have shared earlier, many countries globally have moved towards enacting similar laws and it may be instructive to draw comparisons with the US Committee on Foreign Investment in the US (CFIUS) and the UK's National Security and Investment (NSI) Act.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is as set out in statute at section 721(m) of the Defense Production Act of 1950.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, section 61 of the NSI Act requires an annual report to be published, with minimum statutory requirements relating to the details of its functions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Would the Minister confirm if there will be subsidiary legislation governing the categories of information relating to SIRA that have to be disclosed, to better aid understanding and transparency?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On covered non-controlling investment transactions, these would mean a foreign party investing in a US business involved in critical technology, critical infrastructure and/or sensitive personal data, and the foreign party acquiring at least one of the listed rights.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Further, the Executive Order 14083 specifically identified sectors fundamental to US technological leadership, including but not limited to microelectronics; AI; biotechnology and biomanufacturing; quantum computing; advanced clean energy; climate adaptation technologies; and elements of the agricultural industrial base, that have implications for food security.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The UK NSI has similarly defined the list of 17 sectors of the economy for which prior approval is required for acquisitions that could harm the UK's national security.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In addition to the telecommunications, banking and utilities sectors, in which there are existing sectoral legislation, will the Minister make known the sectors in which SIRA will apply, to provide for greater regulatory transparency to investors and businesses?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Further, given the speed of technological advancements, how often would this sectoral coverage and consequently, the list of designated entities be reviewed and updated?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The UK NSI Act would apply for acquisitions of control over qualifying entities or assets where there could be a potential risk to national security, with control defined as: (a) an entity acquiring or increasing its interest to at least 25% or such that it crosses the 50% or 75% thresholds; (b) an entity acquiring voting rights in qualifying entity such that the acquirer could secure or prevent the passage of any class of resolutions; (c) an entity obtaining “material influence” over a qualifying entity.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise that this is like that of the substantial shareholder notification requirements for listed companies on the Singapore Exchange, but beyond changes in ownership, does the current legislation sufficiently provide for situations where control may be effectively transferred, without necessarily changes in ownership, such as via different classes of shares or specific resolutions that are passed by the company?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, does SIRA also sufficiently cover any technological transfers or core intellectual property rights that may potentially jeopardise our national security, even without ownership changes?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What are the preventive or corrective measures that are available under SIRA to protect these on the grounds of national security?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How then, does the Government satisfy itself that an entity has acted against the national security interests of Singapore?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A law professor was quoted in The Business Times that such an omission is deliberate, and I quote, “to enable the authorities to adopt a broad and generous reading” of the term.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Does the Minister agree with such a view, that such a broad interpretative freedom by the Government was deliberate; and if so, why?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What are the objective and subjective criteria that the Government will put in place in exercising its powers over the key officers of designated entities?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Clause 27(3) references criteria that the Minister may specify; and 27(4) references conditions that the Minister may prescribe for the approval of key officers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What are some examples of and the nature of such criteria and conditions?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We have had a long discussion on the role of judicial review ouster clauses in our legislation, during the debates on the then-Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Bill, or FICA.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: SIRA is similar to FICA, in that there is limited judicial review and in which the reviewing tribunal is also comprised of three individuals appointed by the President on the advice of the Cabinet.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Workers' Party believes in the important oversight mechanism played by the role of the courts and as my hon friend Ms He Ting Ru shared in 2021, such a clause offends Article 93 of the Constitution, which expressly states that "judicial power of Singapore shall be vested in a Supreme Court and in such subordinate courts as may be provided by any written law for the time being in force".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And it is also as important that we continue to uphold and defend the sanctity of the rule of law in Singapore, in which our reputation depends so heavily on.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In a world where some economic activities are intrinsically linked to national security, the importance of this Bill transcends mere financial implications.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is about preserving our sovereignty, protecting our critical infrastructure and ensuring that our nation remains relevant and viable.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I have a few questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: What are the mitigating measures to ensure this Bill does not deter foreign investors and maintains Singapore's reputation as a global investment hub?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How will this affect entities considering investments in infrastructure, technologies or capabilities in Singapore that may be included as significant investments in the future?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How will this process be safeguarded to ensure accountability?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How will this Bill affect entities whose operations depend on specific proprietary technologies and intellectual property whose rights and use may not reside within this entity, and if the network of capabilities or infrastructure is multi-national and cross-border?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is similar to the screening regimes in other countries, such as the UK and Ireland.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progress Singapore Party (PSP) agrees that we can enhance our national security, by ensuring that key entities in critical business sectors always remain under some level of domestic control.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These sectors would include defence, military supplies, telecommunications, transport and banking.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do not oppose setting up a screening regime for ownership transactions in such sensitive sectors of the economy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the powers granted to the Minister to designate entities as critical entities under section 17 of the proposed Bill are very broad, as any entity can be designated as such.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are particularly concerned about the following provisions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will these sensitive economic areas extend to areas which are not considered sensitive in other jurisdictions, such as the media?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The NSI Act in the UK, for example, has subsidiary legislation that designates 17 sensitive areas of the economy, such as AI, defence and transport, where acquisitions must be subject to government review.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the proposed Bill currently provides for the designation of these entities to be publicly announced in the Gazette, it would be better for these economic areas and entities to be designated under a Schedule to the proposed Bill so that Parliament has greater oversight over the designation of these critical entities.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Section 28 of the proposed Bill also allows the Minister to remove key officers in the interest of national security.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP is very concerned about such provisions, which are very broad and could potentially be used by the Government to interfere with the business decisions of private companies or as a tool for retaliation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is, theoretically, possible for the Government to use these powers under section 28 to remove the CEO or director of a critical entity, who has joined an opposition party, in the name of national security interest.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, PSP is concerned by the broad powers of a Police officer to enter premises without a warrant under section 49 of the proposed Bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Government explain why these broad powers are necessary under the proposed Bill, in addition to (a) the power to obtain information by written notice under section 48, of which non-compliance constitutes a criminal offence; and (b) the power of entry with a warrant under section 50?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Judicial review is only allowed under extremely narrow grounds to ensure that the procedures under the Bill, regulations or rules have been complied with.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is also noteworthy that these regulations and rules are made by the Minister himself; and by the Tribunal itself, pursuant to sections 45 and 44(3) of the proposed Bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is very troubling to us that, yet another law is being passed where there is limited provision for judicial review on the grounds of national security.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This ouster clause is very similar to the ouster clauses under the Internal Security Act and FICA.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It breaches the principle of the separation of powers by limiting the checking powers of a co-equal judiciary upholding the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is noteworthy that even in the UK where Parliament is supreme, the National Security and Investment Act 2021 provides for judicial review beyond complaints of procedural improprieties.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP believes that while it is fundamentally in the interest of our national interest to ensure that key entities in critical business entities and business sectors remain under some level of domestic control and can maintain business continuity under all circumstances.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can do this without having such sweeping legal powers on the books.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Recently, we have witnessed several banking and e-payment outages at banks, such as DBS and OCBC, which would be prime candidates to be designated as critical entities under the proposed Bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These banks are already under domestic control and their operations are subject to regulations by the Monetary Authority of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These outages demonstrated that it is not enough to just have oversight over the ownership and management of such entities, if we are really serious about ensuring national security.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There must be a whole-of-country approach towards ensuring the resilience of such critical entities.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, there must be a talent pipeline made up of a strong Singaporean Core that is able to operate, manage and maintain key systems, such as data centres and other IT infrastructure, within critical entities.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also cannot rely excessively on outsourcing these key systems to other foreign countries to save costs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some of these infrastructure and systems must always be maintained in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is in our national interest to ensure that critical entities provide these essential services with minimal and infrequent disruptions in services to the public, even in the absence of extreme situations, such as a war, pandemic or extreme weather caused by climate change.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill follows on the tails of an international wave of jurisdictions introducing or tightening laws with similar intents over the past few years.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I think the Minister mentioned at least 23 countries, but my research seems to suggest that there are over 50 jurisdictions that have done so.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The UK Parliament enacted the NSI Act in 2021, which entered into force in 2022.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In Germany, the government made amendments to the Ordinance on the Designation of Critical Infrastructures, which came into effect in 2022, that significantly expanded the scope of entities that qualify as operators of critical infrastructure and lowered the investment thresholds in certain critical infrastructure sectors, for example, IT, telecommunications and energy.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There are also similar laws in the US and in Australia.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My first clarification is on definitions and the consistency of definitions across statutes.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Personal Data Protection Act, or PDPA, has a definition of "national interest".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is defined as including "national defence, national security, public security, the maintenance of essential services and the conduct of international affairs".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, national security is included in that Act in the definition of "national interest".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: However, I separately note that pursuant to the introduction of FICA, we amended, inter alia, the Societies Act to change the mention of "national interest" to "national security and interest".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It, therefore, follows or suggests that "national security", "national interest" and potentially "national security interest" may actually refer to different things.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I note that in then-Minister for Communications and Information Dr Yaacob Ibrahim's speech on the Films (Amendment) Bill in 2018, the Minister provided another relevant definition, that is, the definition of "considerations of national security".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: He defined it as including what would be "detrimental to the continued existence of the country, its ability to exercise its sovereign rights and the safety and security of citizens and their way of life".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: While it may appear pedantic, it is important for us to have consistency of definitions across statutes, especially when the use of a particular term or particular similar terms confer wide-ranging powers to the respective Minister as it does in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is also important to clarify what exactly the term means to give guidance to the Office of Significant Investments Review, which will be set up after the enactment of the Bill, on what exactly are the activities they should be looking out for, particularly as regards non-designated entities that have acted against Singapore's national interests, pursuant to clause 32 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It would also help to identify what activities or transactions entities should avoid so that they are not inadvertently caught by the provisions of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Again, I would like to emphasise that consistency in the use of terms across statutes is important and that these definitions should be clarified at the earliest opportunity to avoid ambiguity and uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, the point made by the hon Non-Constituency Member of Parliament Mr Leong just in his speech before mine is interesting, where he asked whether a CEO who joined an opposition party, whether such a situation would be considered as contrary to national security.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, if we can define what the term is properly and clearly, then we can avoid such concerns or such assertions being made, which may mislead the public as to the intentions and the results of the application of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My second question is with regard to the possibility of listed companies being designated as designated entities, in particular, defence-related Singapore-listed companies.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I note that the list of designated companies will be published after the enactment of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: First, I expect that the mere fact that a company is a listed company would not deter the Government from designating it as a designated entity if necessary.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has shown how important it is that we have control over critical entities, supply sources and logistic chains.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given how dependent we are on imports and considering the diversity of countries which supply goods and services to Singapore, we must ensure that significant investments are from reliable and friendly allies to mitigate our risks.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   The proposed Bill is intended to complement the existing legislation that already targets individual business sectors, while the current legislation already imposes restrictions on institutions in sectors, such as telecommunications, banking and utilities.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, since these institutions have not been identified, would the Minister be able to share more clearly the criteria for the selection or exclusion of these candidates and the components which buyers and sellers need to pay attention to?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will the Minister provide more information and examples of the circumstances under which our national security and strategic interests are threatened?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Do these instances include private healthcare facilities with medical records of our government leaders and industry heads?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This new Bill should draw upon experiences from the past and most importantly, not cause foreign investors to lose confidence in Singapore, which impact employment opportunities for our people. : Another question I have is regarding the complex structures of many investment companies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: More likely than not, most have many owners and the intertwined relationships can be multi-layered and multinational.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How would the Government assess these complicated fund sources and identify the ultimate beneficiary owners?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the event remedial direction may be issued to transfer or dispose equity interests held in the designated entities or to change a key office-bearer, how does the Minister decide on the timeframe?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A lot of malicious corporate actions can be performed during a short duration.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As with any new process, there are possibilities of unintended consequences.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a country, which has traditionally courted investments, how would the Government project our continued welcome of legitimate investments and build upon our reputation as an attractive investment destination?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Before us today is the Significant Investments Review Bill.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Keeping in context the current geopolitical environment, many similar open economies in the world have introduced measures to subject investments in strategically important companies to greater scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: There is a concern that investments in strategic companies may be motivated not just by commercial interests, but also by geopolitical objectives.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: These concerns are most pronounced where the acquiring firms are state-owned or controlled by a state.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, considering Singapore's status as a significant global financial hub that embraces international investors, conducting such a review at this time is highly opportune.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Clarity and consistency of policy is what sophisticated investors around the world look for.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Striking a balance between ensuring national security and maintaining a business-friendly environment is crucial for enhancing Singapore's competitiveness in the global arena.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill empowers the Minister to take various actions, including designating entities, issuing remedial actions and conducting reviews of transactions.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The potential for such an intervention may result in delays in the approval of forthcoming legitimate investments.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister please elaborate on the scenarios that may warrant some of these remedial actions?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Has a maximum timeline been provided for issuing remedial decisions and conducting reviews of transactions?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Also, has a timeline been established for the regular review of the list of designated entities?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Another point where I would like to seek a clarification on, is what may constitute national security interests?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: While I fully appreciate it may be impossible to list every possible interest, I ask for this clarification as, in many other jurisdictions, the ambiguity surrounding this definition has led to significant losses for investors.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In the current geopolitical environment, the biggest national threat for Singapore is the economic threat.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As has been mentioned, this new legislation will be in addition to the existing sectoral legislation in regulated sectors, such as telecommunications, banking and utilities.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Would we not have been better served by having one clear, consistent and comprehensive Bill that covers all relevant sectors and entities?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: From a business investor's point of view, having one single comprehensive process would provide the enhanced clarity and consistency that is desired.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I would like to seek a clarification on whether a more comprehensive approach to regulating foreign investments in entities significant to Singaporeans' daily lives is being considered.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: For example, in Australia, the Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers Act 1975 applies to all foreign investments in that country.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Having a similar act would help maintain all critical entities that play a key role in the daily life of all Singaporeans to remain in control of Singaporeans rather than fall prey in the hands of foreign investors who, perhaps, may be more focused on short-term profits rather than optimising quality products and services for Singaporeans over the long-term.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Establishing such a higher minimum transaction value could perhaps help maintain efficiency without compromising regulatory oversight and continue to make Singapore an attractive destination for foreign investment.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In summary, aiming to enhance the resilience of the economy and strengthen Singapore's position as a trusted hub for businesses to invest with confidence, in my view, the introduction of SIRB at this time is opportune and excellent for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill provides the necessary flexibility to the Minister to act swiftly and decisively when needed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This is an important, timely and strategic Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill develops an investment management regime that balances Singapore's economic prosperity and capacity to attract investors with proportional oversight mechanisms to protect and safeguard Singapore's national security interests.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As explained by Minister Gan earlier, this Bill aims to adopt a calibrated approach, balancing both investment and national security interests.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is a small nation with no natural resources to trade with the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, we have developed a robust economy and established a strong reputation in global markets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We have created a safe and secure environment for our people with living standards that are among the highest in the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We have come a long way over the past 60 years: from our initial industrialisation effort in the 1960s, with factories producing items, such as garments, mosquito coils and toys; to now, hosting regional headquarters for some of the world's largest and most innovative companies, such as Novartis, Microsoft and Apple.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Issues of national security are multifaceted and constantly evolving in an interconnected world where capital flows transcend borders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The impact of large investments on nationals' well-being cannot be understated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Certain industries are critical to Singapore's infrastructure and our safety and security must be shielded from potential threats posed by foreign and domestic entities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Legislative control is necessary to prevent large-scale disruptions to critical entities caused by speculative investments or hostile takeovers, without compromising Singapore's attractiveness to foreign investors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: With that understanding and while I acknowledge the potential benefits of this Bill, I do have some clarifications and suggestions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: My concerns are largely based on my research and development of courses related to this topic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Prof Arnold Wolfers from Yale University famously defined national security as an ambiguous symbol.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: According to Prof Wolfers, "National security concerns the protection or preservation of cherished values against threat or damage and traditionally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: For the State, these values are sovereignty and prosperity".

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Prof Wolfers goes on to say that, "In an objective sense, national security measures the absence of threats to acquired values; in a subjective sense, it measures the absence of fear that such values will be attacked." Given the inherent vagueness surrounding the terms "national security" and "national security interests" and the ever-changing nature of national security, it may not be feasible to include a workable definition of those terms in the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, I would like to echo the points made by my fellow Nominated Member of Parliament, Mr Raj Thomas, on the need to differentiate the terms and be clear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, what is a national security issue one day, may not be so the next; and we also never know what is around the corner regarding new and emerging national security threats.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We have the National Security Coordination Secretariat that provides planning and coordination and each Ministry also has its own system for assessing risk to national security.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In doing so, the tool could also be used to assess or categorise investments based on their potential impact on national security as well as monitor which sectors may pose a greater security risk at any one time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As well as being of assistance across the Government, the risk assessment tool could also form the basis of guidelines to educate and support potential investors with investment applications.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The guidelines would also promote responsible investments, increase investors' confidence in expanding into sensitive industries and maintain the image of Singapore as being efficient and pro-business.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Being legislatively based would clarify and formalise the roles and function of the office and would provide the office with ongoing certainty and stability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It would not be helpful if investors, either current or future, felt that the only function of the office was to oversee, investigate and issue remedial opinionative directions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I am pleased to note that this Bill provides information on the administration, reconsideration, appeals and judicial review as well as enforcement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is important for any remedial opinionative direction made to be transparent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: By doing so, I believe we can create a safe environment, promoting responsible investments and voluntary compliance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: To conclude, this Bill is a positive step forward in ensuring Singapore remains a resilient and secured nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: When developing this management review framework, we must strike a balance between considering global economic condition, geopolitical tensions, defer competition for investments and investors' aspirations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first set of clarifications, is on the notification and approval regime for notification and approval regime for controllers of designated entities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under section 16, a person's shareholdings are combined with their associates' shareholdings to determine if notice or approval requirements are triggered.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The definition of associate, under section 15, is very wide.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It can include even a person's employers, employees and colleagues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share how the monitoring of the shareholding of associates may be carried out in practice by individuals?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If there is any contravention of notices or approval requirements, the burden is on the accused to prove that they were not aware of the contravention.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister also provide examples of what an accused will need to show to prove that they were not aware of the contravention?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My other clarification on this topic, is on a difference in the defences available for contravening certain notices requirements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify the rationale for making it is easier to avail to the defence in section 19?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second clarification is on the Minister's power to issue a review notice against an entity that has acted against our national security interests.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This power extends beyond designated entities, to any entity formed in or carrying business in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It also extends to any transaction where voting power is acquired.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MTI has said that the Bill is designed to be business-friendly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, these broad powers may increase costs and slow down business activity by requiring additional due diligence and monitoring of investments after a transaction has closed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share the findings of its consultations with businesses on the impact of these provisions and how the Government intends to mitigate the impact on businesses?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My last clarification is on the role and powers of the Reviewing Tribunal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The proceedings of a Reviewing Tribunal are deemed to be judicial proceedings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister confirm that the Reviewing Tribunal will apply consistent standards of judicial review as the Singapore Courts, with reference to the applicable case precedents?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Due to national security reasons also, appellants may not be provided with full information regarding the decision being appealed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister confirm that the Reviewing Tribunal will be separately provided with all information, even information not given to the appellant, to make their decision?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, will the Reviewing Tribunal be allowed to take into account the potentially incomplete information provided to the appellant, in deciding each case?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, our decision to keep supply chains open and maintain trade links not only demonstrated our resilience but also reinforced worldwide investors' confidence.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This strategic move was crucial at a time when many countries were turning inwards, underscoring Singapore's role as a reliable partner in global trade and commerce.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As we navigate new geopolitical and security complexities, it is crucial that the Significant Investments Review Bill is crafted and perceived as an extension of these values.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill must be seen as a proactive measure to safeguard our economic and security interests while reinforcing our commitment to being an open, transparent and reliable partner in the global economy.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As mentioned by the Minister, many countries have established various forms of investment screening, particularly in sensitive sectors, such as defence, technology, infrastructure and energy, reflecting the global trend towards safeguarding national interest.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: One of our nearest neighbours, Vietnam, has investment management rules for critical sectors, like rice exports and mineral mining.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses appreciate that the proposed Bill strikes a reasonable balance between national security needs and business priorities.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is not an omnibus legislation and will only be applied to a handful of designated entities critical to Singapore's national security interests.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This will give great comfort to ensure existing investors do not get stuck and entrepreneurs not lose value from having a narrower group of investors to prospect for fundraising or exit.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The publication of the list of the designated entities will also be important to take the guesswork out of potential investors.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Under what circumstances and how often will the designated list be updated?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Under the provisions regarding national security interest directions that the proposed Bill permits, the definition of national security needs further clarity as spoken by Nominated Member Raj Thomas.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is not ideal especially for higher-value transactions and investments.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Second, there are powers under this Bill that allow for the review of ownership of entities even if they are not designated.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: There are concerns that this will give the Government "soft" powers to flag and control the transactions of legitimate entities in certain sectors.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It would be helpful for the Government to provide more clarity on how businesses can have certainty that they would not be penalised under this legislation and the conditions that they would have to fulfil do not fall out of line with national security provisions.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The current requirements under section 32(1), which provide that the Minister's powers can activated as long as the entity is incorporated and has business activity in Singapore, are quite broad and arguably require further clarity.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, we call for a consistently open and consultative approach from the Government, including established timelines for responses and a transparent appeals process.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This will enable businesses to effectively navigate the legislation and align their operations with national security requirements.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We appreciate that under section 28, designated entities and affected individuals will be given an opportunity to be heard in decisions regarding removal of key officers.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It would be ideal if a similar forum could be provided for other Orders made under the proposed Bill as well.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We need to ensure that companies, investors and entrepreneurs do not perceive this proposed Bill as a protectionist move by Singapore, as such ownership rules tend to be associated with these intentions.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed Bill does well by clarifying the limited circumstances in which the Minister's discretion may be exercised and provides well-needed assurance that orders made outside such purposes would be against the spirit and objective of the Act under section 29(2).

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In doing so, we can continue to strengthen Singapore's position as a trusted hub for businesses and investments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, I seek clarifications on how the Bill may impact foreign investment and some specific industries.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One of my primary concerns lies in the potential dampening effect this Bill may pose to foreign investment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: At present, the lack of specific guidelines could create an environment of uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While we understand the need for discretion, without a clear understanding of the risk assessment methodology, investors might hesitate and this might impede economic growth.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Also, will the provisions of this Bill conflict with any existing trade agreements?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If so, how will this be addressed when the provisions of this Bill become law?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Speaker, Sir, the broad authority granted to the Government under this Bill raises legitimate questions about transparency and accountability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is to reassure stakeholders that they may be assured of equitable and judicious application of this law, thereby averting the potential abuse of authority.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, how does the Minister intend to strike a balance between security and economic growth?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Achieving equilibrium between national security imperatives and economic prosperity is a nuanced undertaking.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Compliance, like a tangled vine, can choke the life out of economic activity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must ensure that the burden placed on designated entities is proportionate to the identified risk, lest we inadvertently stifle the very growth that we seek to protect.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government provide concrete examples of how the Bill will affect businesses in different sectors?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What measures are in place to minimise compliance costs and administrative burdens?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must treat them with the care they deserve.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Overly stringent regulations risk stifling innovation and hampering our capacity to attract and retain talent, as the designated entities are required to seek approval for the appointment of key officers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, this may ultimately hinder our long-term economic objectives.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mr Speaker, Sir, did we learn from the experiences of other countries with similar legislation, in the formulation of this Bill?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I note that some countries have acknowledged the need to have adequate levers to ensure the security and reliability of their critical infrastructure, facilities, supply chains, technologies and resources.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The transaction was deemed a potential risk to national security.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
