text: This was because of the critical national security and defence capabilities relating to naval propulsion systems delivered through the two UK entities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While the acquisition was eventually given the go-ahead, it was subject to various conditions, such as physical and information security requirements.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must, therefore, look beyond our shores and other similar legislation implemented overseas.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For instance, how do other countries define "national security interests"?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What safeguards have they put in place to ensure transparency and accountability?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By learning from others, we can refine our own Bill to achieve its objectives without inadvertently harming our economic engine.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fifth, Mr Speaker, Sir, consideration should be given to the protection of minority shareholders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill must, where possible, ensure the fair treatment and protection of these shareholders within designated entities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Their investments should not be prejudiced beyond what is necessary.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Clear guidelines and robust dispute resolution mechanisms must be established to safeguard their interests.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, Mr Speaker, Sir, how does the Government ensure clarity and efficiency of the review process?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It must be a process that is streamlined, expeditious and without unnecessary delays or administrative burdens.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Investors deserve a transparent and timely decision-making process, one that fosters trust and encourages continued engagement with our economy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government elaborate on the safeguards against potential misuse of Ministerial powers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be independent review mechanisms in place for Ministerial decisions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Also, can the Government assure us that the Tribunal will be equipped with the necessary expertise to handle complex national security considerations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will its decisions be binding on the Minister?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Further, will the Government publish or share the findings and the basis of such reviews?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Doing so will likely instil confidence in investors, so that they may trust that such a process is transparent and fair.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What additional manpower would be required by this office?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And given that this deals with national security interests would it mean only Singapore citizens would be employed?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One path leads to a fortress, our nation shielded from harm.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But another path leads to a tangled thicket, growth choked by uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, I urge the Government to carefully consider the clarifications offered, scrutinise the potential ramifications of the Bill and glean valuable insights from the experiences of other countries.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Only through comprehensive deliberation can we refine this legislation into a robust shield that protects our national interests without stifling innovation and investment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It also reaffirms Singapore's commitment to being a beacon of transparency, fairness, and a thriving economic engine for generations to come.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us ensure that this legislation protects our future, not impedes it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us act now, without hesitation, to weave a future where security and prosperity flourish side by side.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As the global economic and political landscape becomes increasingly volatile, I agree that it is timely that we further tighten the oversight of critical entities that are crucial to the proper functioning of our economy and society.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singapore must guard against undue influence from players whose interests may not be aligned with ours.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As we debate the Significant Investments Review Bill, we should be reminded of instances when Singapore was on the receiving end of such considerations.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The takeover was deemed not to be in Australia's national interest.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With the introduction of Significant Investments Review Bill, Singapore will align with numerous countries globally that have strengthened their investment management legislation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Those in the investor community that I spoke to, whilst initially surprised by this introduction, acknowledged and said they understand the necessity of such measures in the context of today's economic environment.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As highlighted in the 2023 United Nations Article on "The Evolution of FDI Screening Mechanisms", it is important to find the proper balance between preserving an appropriate level of regulatory discretion to address national security challenges while ensuring an acceptable level of certainty and predictability to investors.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Three crucial aspects – predictability, transparency and administrative efficiency – are key to effective implementation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To achieve this, it is of utmost importance that the provisions in the Bill adopt a balanced rules-based approach, with a predictable screening process with minimal bureaucracy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Bill should also align with international best practices and standards, be focused on high-risk entities and never, never over-extend its regime.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We should also take into consideration how the Bill may impact the wider investor community, including minority shareholders.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With these factors in mind, I would like to make five key points pertaining to the Bill.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: First, it is noteworthy that the provisions in the Significant Investments Review Bill apply to both local and foreign investors, based primarily on considerations of national security.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This approach prevents potential biases or preferential treatment that could disadvantage either domestic or foreign investors, fostering a level playing field and enhancing transparency in the investment environment.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The distinction between foreign and local can also sometimes be arbitrary.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, knowing that all players are subject to the same scrutiny can reassure investors that the market operates under fair and transparent principles.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Without a clear definition of what constitutes "national security interests", this may risk the new regime being seen as opaque, lacking in transparency and fuel investors' fear of the enforcement being arbitrary.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I do acknowledge the multifaceted dimensions of what national security might entail, and Singapore has our own unique security needs, economic structure and geopolitical context.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For example, the UK's NSI Act identifies 17 sensitive sectors where acquisitions need to be notified for national security reasons.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But there is great, great merit in increased transparency around what is deemed as critical entities and this would be enhanced by a regular process of providing detailed decisions by which others could judge how the process operates.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Third, the designation and approval process must be efficient and streamlined with minimal bureaucracy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I appreciate the Bill sets out clear and detailed processes, including instances where affected parties will have the opportunities to submit representations before the Minister makes his decisions; and there are channels for reconsideration requests and appeals to an independent Reviewing Tribunal.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Minister also mentioned in his Second Reading speech, that there will be a dedicated one-stop office that will be set up to provide guidance as well as address clarifications from affected stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I think this dedicated touchpoint is helpful and reassuring.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, while Bill does stipulate expected turnaround time for designated entities to respond to the authorities, the other way round is absent – so the expected turnaround time from the Minister or the authorities to revert for approvals and appeals is unclear.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As business transactions are often time-sensitive, it would be reasonable to consider providing clarity on turnaround times for approvals and appeals, so that companies may make the necessary arrangements to meet the requirements under the Bill as well as their own business obligations.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: If necessary, this can be followed by a further 45-day investigation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The members are also accorded judicial protection and immunity as a Judge of the High Court and decisions made by the Tribunal are deemed as judicial proceedings.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: At the same time, members of the Reviewing Tribunal will have access to information in the areas of internal security, defence, technology, national security and commerce.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These stipulations reflect the highest importance and emphasis placed on the Reviewing Tribunal.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How can the investor community be confident that the Reviewing Tribunal members are free from political and economic pressures influencing the review process?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Fourth, it is of utmost importance that the application of the Significant Investments Review process is focused on high-risk entities and never to over-extend its regime.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Significant Investments Review Bill is expected to be targeted and imposed on individual entities not covered by existing sectoral legislation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Could the Minister please clarify, how the sector-specific legislation will be effectively integrated with the Significant Investment Review legislation?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In light of the additional obligations that come with being identified as a critical entity, will the Government consider implementing compensatory measures to ensure these entities can effectively meet their responsibilities?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For example, could a large data centre infrastructure, designated as a critical entity, be assured of priority access to electricity to maintain uninterrupted operations vital to its role?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Fifth, as the Bill entails a range of possible interventions ranging from divestment orders to remedial directions around equity interests and control over officers of designated entities, such actions may have implications on market perception and confidence of the designated entities' future performance and prospects.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I am concerned about the impact to minority shareholders.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For example, blocking a foreign acquisition may prevent a potential increase in share price, affecting potential gains for minority shareholders.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In some cases, the Government intervention might lead to liquidity concerns, especially if it involves critical sectors where investment options are limited.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This could affect the ability of minority shareholders to sell their shares without incurring significant losses.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How can the Government protect the rights of minority shareholders in such circumstances?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For example, in cases where the Government intervention leads to expropriation or nationalisation, will it ensure that minority shareholders receive fair compensation for their shares?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To conclude, beyond the specifics hard-coded in legislation, it is imperative to recognise that, for businesses and investors, the consistent application of transparency in interactions with stakeholders after the Bill's passage holds paramount importance.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The true measure of our conduct will be reflected in the investors' actual experiences with the authorities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This includes the efficiency with which their applications are processed and the openness of regulators regarding the progress and status of these applications.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singapore boasts an exemplary track record of administrative efficiency.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, I hope the Ministry will maintain this standard of efficiency in the implementation of this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I note that Mr Leong Mun Wai has not supported the Bill and I hope I can explain to him all his questions, and I hope he will reconsider his decision.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Allow me to now address some of the key points and questions Members have raised.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In developing the Bill, we have studied carefully the investment management legislation of other jurisdictions as well as our own current sectoral legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Bill's provisions are largely similar to those in overseas legislation and are quite similar to those in our existing sectoral legislation, which most investors would therefore be familiar with.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These provisions are also consistent with our international trade obligations, a concern raised by several Members.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have reached out to various local and international communities to explain the intent of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have reassured them that the Bill has been carefully calibrated to balance between having adequate oversight over the ownership and control of these critical entities, while ensuring that Singapore's economy remains open and business-friendly, as well as investor-friendly.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will address the concerns raised by Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Shawn Huang and Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Don Wee asked about the impact of existing sectoral legislation on companies in sectors, such as utilities and banking.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: While this will be more appropriately addressed by the respective sector lead agencies, I can assure Mr Wee that they have been working closely with the industry to address their concerns and minimise any adverse impact.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Neil Parekh, Assoc Prof Razwana Begum, Mr Raj Thomas and Mr Louis Chua have all asked for greater clarity on the definition of "national security".

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Having discussed and deliberated extensively – internally and with our advisors and various parties – and taking into account legislation introduced by other jurisdictions; I came to a conclusion that sometimes, less is more.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Especially, in today's world where the global landscape changes very quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: National security considerations will evolve over time, and we need to keep the scope wide to allow us sufficient flexibility so that we can respond to unanticipated circumstances in good time.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Having said that, broadly speaking, in the context of the Bill, national security would cover areas critical to Singapore's sovereignty and security, including our economic security and the continued delivery of our essential services.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As I have mentioned in my Second Reading speech, an example would be if an entity is a key provider of security-related functions, especially where there are few or no alternatives, then this entity will be a critical entity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Neil Parekh asked how sector-specific legislation will interact with the new Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Sectoral legislation is intended to address sector-specific considerations, including those beyond national security interests, and may set out different obligations than those under this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Bill is intended to complement existing legislation and focus mainly on national security-related issues.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Shawn Huang and Mr Leong Mun Wai asked how the Bill will affect designated entities' operations, capabilities and infrastructure.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As mentioned in my Second Reading speech, the Bill's provisions relate only to ownership and control over designated entities and the Government has no intention to directly interfere with routine commercial decisions and operations of the designated entities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Ms Foo Mee Har, Mr Don Wee and Mr Shawn Huang asked about specific factors that will be taken into consideration in designating entities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Leong also asked which sectors will be covered by this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I have covered this in my Second Reading speech.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To reiterate, we do not intend to designate specific sectors, but rather, we will designate specific entities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Considerations would include, whether the entity provides a critical function in relation to Singapore's national security interests and whether the entity is adequately covered by sectoral legislation already.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Neil Parekh asked whether there will be inconsistencies in regulation of entities with a similar economic risk profile.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Entities with similar profiles and importance to our national security interests will generally be equally considered for designation, although there may be other considerations that eventually result in different designation decisions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng, Ms Foo Mee Har, Mr Don Wee, Mr Neil Parekh, Mr Raj Thomas and Mr Louis Chua asked about potential entities that may be designated.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As most critical entities in Singapore are already adequately covered by existing sectoral legislation, we expect only a handful of critical entities to be designated under this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Designated entities who are of the view that they no longer meet the designation criteria may also engage the Office of Significant Investments Review to request for a review of their designation status.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I would encourage Members not to speculate at this point, which particular entities will be designated.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: And as mentioned in my Second Reading speech, after the Act comes into force, all designations will be notified in the Gazette.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We intend to review the list and carry out assessments from time to time, as required.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Ministry will be judicious in exercising the powers under the Act and set out clear processes where possible, to minimise the overall impact on businesses and investors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: On the specific obligations under the Bill, Mr Don Wee asked how the Government will assess complicated fund sources and identify the beneficial owners.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will be as thorough as possible, including consolidating and making sense of information from various sources.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But I concede that there will indeed be challenges in detecting instances of non-compliance when ownership structures are complex.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is, indeed, why we need adequate flexibility to be able to respond to emerging national security threats.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Louis Ng commented that the definition of "associates" under the Bill is very wide.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The definition is actually quite clearly set out in the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, those with familial relations or employees of the same employer would be deemed as "associates".

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked how monitoring of shareholding of one's associates may be carried out in practice by individuals.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In practice, if an incoming controller is an individual and is aware that its associates also have shareholding in the designated entities, it should take active steps to ensure that it is able to comply with the notification and approval requirements.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, it could reach out to its associates and request that all parties update each other if they plan to make any changes to their respective shareholding.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked for examples of what a non-compliant party will need to show to prove that they were not aware of a contravention.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This would be fact-dependent, depending on the specific facts and circumstances of each case.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: If, for example, the contravention occurred due to active action on the part of its associates, then the accused will likely need to demonstrate that it had no prior knowledge of this.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For completeness, even if an accused successfully proves that it was not aware of the contravention when it occurred, to avail itself of the defence, it will have to comply with other provisions in the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These include, notifying the Minister of the contravention within the specified period after he has become aware of it and complying with the remedial directions that the Minister might have issued.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked why the thresholds for defence differ for similar provisions across clauses 18 and 19.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The thresholds are different as they were set, taking into account the contexts and other associated measures.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Louis Chua asked about the rationale for notification obligations that are applicable to 5% controllers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As the Member has pointed out, this is like that of the "substantial shareholder" definition in other legislation, such as the Companies Act and the Securities and Futures Act.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will allow the Minister to know that someone has now become a substantial shareholder in an entity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Louis Chua also asked if the Bill sufficiently covers various scenarios under which control may be effectively transferred, such as via different classes of shares or specific resolutions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: On his cited example where this is done via different classes of shares, the direct control thresholds may apply, as they are determined based on holding of equity interests or voting power in the designated entity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: On his other example where this is done via specific resolution, the approval obligations relating to indirect control would be also applicable.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is based on qualitative tests of control, for example, whether parties are able to determine the policy of the designated entity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Neil Parekh asked about scenarios that may warrant remedial directions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, a party may be ordered to transfer or dispose of equity interests held in the designated entities, if conditions of approval have not been complied with.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Don Wee asked about the considerations underlying the Minister's decision on the timeframe stated in the remedial directions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Minister will take into account all relevant factors and circumstances of each case.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This would include balancing between addressing the extent of national security risk or harm and affording the parties reasonable time to perform the necessary action.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Louis Chua asked about the factors that the Minister could consider in assessing the appointment or removal of key personnel.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As mentioned in the example in my Second Reading speech, if we receive information that an individual has a track record of engaging in conduct or activities that could undermine our national security interests, then this would be taken into consideration.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Mark Lee and Mr Neil Parekh raised concerns about the clarity and efficiency of review processes.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is because they may be diverse and complex considerations relating to specific cases.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Minister should be allowed adequate time to conduct thorough assessments.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: And as mentioned in my Second Reading speech, we will set up a dedicated office under the Ministry.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The office will work closely with the designated entities and affected parties.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will endeavour to process all applications expeditiously and avoid undue delays.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Applicants are also welcome to check in with the office on the progress of their applications.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Yip Hon Weng raised concerns about the impact of ownership and control provisions on designated entities, especially on minority shareholders.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, for the Special Administration Order involving the transfer of property, rights and liabilities from the designated entity to a prescribed transferee, a payment scheme will also be established to determine the amount of payment to be made.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Louis Ng, Mr Mark Lee and Mr Louis Chua have raised clarifications about the powers that can be exercised against any entity that has acted against the national security interests.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have consulted key stakeholders and they generally recognise the need for the powers to take action against any entity that have acted against our national security interests, even if they have not been designated under the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: They understood it should apply only to very few entities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We do not expect there to be significant economic impact on the vast majority of non-designated entities, which have no proactive obligation to track, monitor or report transactions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As I have mentioned in my Second Reading speech, currently under the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act, the Court may order the winding up of a company if it is used against Singapore's national security.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Bill provides a more appropriate and calibrated approach than winding up the company.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Following the review of the transaction under the Bill, directions may be issued, such as directing the transacting party to transfer or dispose of his equity interest in the entity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will allow the entity to directly address the risk or harm, while continuing to operate.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa had a query about the considerations behind the two-year time bar.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The two-year time bar seeks to strike a balance between providing a sufficient runway to commence a review under the Bill and giving investors certainty as to when transactions would no longer be subject to such powers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Relatedly, Mr Mark Lee said that notwithstanding the time bar for the Minister's issuance of a review notice, there is no time limit for Minister's directions thereafter.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We should ensure that the Minister has adequate time to conduct thorough assessments, as I have mentioned earlier, as well as carefully consider what appropriate directions ought to be issued.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Nonetheless, let me assure Members that the Government will endeavour to resolve such national security-related matters expeditiously.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Louis Chua had a specific query on how the Government will satisfy itself that an entity has acted against our national security interests.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will be dependent on the circumstances of the case.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As mentioned in my Second Reading speech, the Minister for Home Affairs can also issue a certificate stating that he is satisfied that the entity has acted so.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked if the Government will publish its decisions and the basis for doing so.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Notwithstanding this, we may do so on a discretionary basis depending on the case-specific circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Louis Chua cited the examples of the publication of annual reports in overseas jurisdictions and asked if we will have subsidiary legislation on disclosure of information relating to the Bill's implementation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Given that we intend to designate only a handful of entities under the Act and such designation will be notified in the Gazette, there may not be a need for the publication of an annual report per se.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Shawn Huang and Mr Mark Lee raised the need for safeguards and a robust oversight mechanism.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Any aggrieved party can seek reconsideration from the Minister for his decisions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: They may also further appeal to an independent Reviewing Tribunal.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Yip Hon Weng raised specific queries about the composition of the Reviewing Tribunal.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will consult the Chief Justice on the nomination of the Supreme Court Judges, who will serve as chairpersons of the Reviewing Tribunal.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The other members of the Reviewing Tribunal will be selected based on their areas of expertise and standing, just like any other tribunals or independent committees.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To ensure independent decision-making by members of the Reviewing Tribunal, the Bill expressly states that the Minister cannot alter the remuneration and terms of service to their disadvantage once they are appointed by the President.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Further, as Ms Foo Mee Har has highlighted, members of the Reviewing Tribunal will also have the same legal protection and immunity as a High Court Judge.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if the Reviewing Tribunal will be separately provided with all information, including information that may not be disclosed to the appellant, to make their decisions; and if so, whether the Reviewing Tribunal can take this into account when deciding on the appeal.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Yes, the intent is to ensure that appeals before a Reviewing Tribunal are properly heard and thoroughly considered.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will also be working out the rules of the Tribunal in the coming months, which will be published in the subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked whether the Reviewing Tribunal's decision will be binding on the Minister.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Louis Chua and Mr Leong Mun Wai asked about the limited judicial review provision in the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I should reiterate that parties can already appeal to the Reviewing Tribunal on decisions by the Minister.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In response to Mr Mark Lee, yes, parties can also appeal to the Tribunal on Special Administration Orders.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai also asked about Police powers and why they should be given the powers to enter premises without warrant to carry out their investigations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This power is already consistent with the powers given to the Police under the Criminal Procedure Code, as well as many other domestic legislations to allow them to carry out their investigations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In matters relating to national security, these matters are time-sensitive and it is important to allow the Police officers and commercial affairs officers the flexibility and the ability to carry out their investigation in relation to this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Office will also serve as a dedicated one-stop touchpoint and closely engage all stakeholders to address their concerns and to minimise the impact on them, if any.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Bill will strengthen our position as a trusted hub for businesses to invest with confidence in a stable, safe and secure Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It provides an updated toolkit of levers to enhance our economic resilience and strengthen national security amidst a rapidly evolving and increasingly complex operating landscape.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: At the same time, I agree with Mr Mark Lee and Mr Don Wee that we should continue to build on our key fundamentals and strengths which underpin our attractiveness as a business hub, to capture new opportunities and support our businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are doing so through three broad strategies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: First, expanding and deepening economic connectivity for Singapore through international economic partnerships and agreements.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Second, renewing Singapore's relevance to the world by furthering cooperation in strategic growth areas, such as sustainability and digitalisation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Third, remaining open as well as protecting Singapore's access to key resources and preferential trade status, by leveraging existing and new collaborations; as well as international engagements.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will continue to establish strong supply ecosystems and work with businesses, including encouraging them to adopt supply chain resilience efforts, such as diversification of sources to better cope with global supply chain disruptions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As a small and open economy, Singapore will need to keep at adapting our economic strategies in response to the changing global landscape.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I am heartened that Members have acknowledged the necessity and importance of this Bill, and support the Ministry's approach in balancing between economic growth and national security considerations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: With the support of the House today, this Bill will strengthen Singapore's position as a trusted hub for businesses to invest with confidence.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, would you like for your dissent to be recorded?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I did not mean to stop the formation of the Committee of the whole House.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Which was the question I had raised earlier, and I asked whether the ayes have it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I raised my voice because I thought it was for objecting to the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can I register my objection to the Bill?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Can I suggest that when we go to the Reading of the Bill later, we register your dissent there?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 3.20 pm until 3.40 pm.
